tldr: A bank mainframe-to-Kafka proof of concept was vibe-coded to a demo, then made production-grade by surrounding the agents with deterministic harnesses: build enforcers, OpenRewrite, ArchUnit, scripts and token discipline.
summary: Anyul Rivas (GFT) tells the story in three film-themed chapters. In 'Limitless', three architects had to show a bank how to stream a COBOL mainframe's transactions from SQL Server through Debezium change data capture into Kafka, consumed by Java and C# microservices using the outbox pattern and dead-letter queues, on OpenShift with Helm and Azure DevOps. The bank allowed only Artifactory dependencies, no outside images, no skills, MCP servers or sub-agents, and at first no AI traces in the repo; GitHub Copilot came later. With roughly a month left after onboarding, they vibe-coded a working demo: by Rivas's count 25k commits, 3,500 auto-merged pull requests and 180,000 generated lines.

Vague user stories invite hallucination, so the team ran Matt Pocock's 'grill me' skill to turn each story into an implementation-ready spec with edge cases, bank constraints and acceptance evidence that tells the agent when to stop. The client rejected OpenSpec-style tools and wanted ADRs kept in Confluence, so the team built its own research-plan-implement workflow ending in a mandatory sync of Azure DevOps stories and Confluence pages. They ran two tracks: vibe coding to reach and validate the demo, then a separate engineered track for production. Rivas frames this with John Ousterhout's tactical versus strategic programming.

The 'Apollo 13' chapter treats the harness as the adapter that makes a stochastic model fit deterministic production rules. Lessons included: Maven Enforcer to stop models silently downgrading Java 25 to 17; positive (cataphatic) rather than negative (apophatic) instructions; context engineering after the bank said three people were using 30% of the company's monthly Copilot quota; a duplication threshold in the build; OpenRewrite recipes for style; ArchUnit and ArchUnit.NET for the bank's layering; CLI calls instead of forbidden MCP servers for Confluence; and a per-environment provisioning script for SQL Server under Rosetta. Role-based sub-agent teams and naive TDD both failed.

In the 'Matrix' chapter Rivas argues the developer moves from Neo, fighting inside the code, to Tank on the Nebuchadnezzar: providing judgement, constraints, tools, environments and clear stop conditions while agents handle the tactical work. He cites a study of 660 Claude Code runs in which clean code did not change pass rates but cut tokens and file revisits. He closes with a work-in-progress 'AI harness scorecard' script that rates a repository on five pillars. In Q&A he said the production phase grew to more than 100 bank developers consuming the SDK.
keyPoints: Vibe coding was used deliberately from idea to demo; production quality came from a second track with engineering practices, not from continuing to prompt the prototype.
A 300-line implementation plan is cheaper to review than a 5,000-10,000-line pull request, so the human review effort goes into the grilled spec and plan.

Recurring agent mistakes became build failures: Maven Enforcer for the Java version, banned dependencies and groupId/artifactId patterns; a duplication threshold with a message telling the agent to refactor; OpenRewrite recipes (Mockito, AssertJ, Testcontainers, idiomatic Java); ArchUnit tests for architecture layers.

Token discipline: the RTK CLI proxy (Rivas credits it with 60-80% savings), AGENTS.md files under 500 lines, archived stale ADRs, a new session per task kept around 70% context use, skills loaded on demand, an LSP or CodeGraph map instead of rescanning code, and capped output tokens, which cost three to eight times more than input.
A 'virtual IT department' of front-end, back-end, DevOps and QA sub-agents failed, with most tokens spent on agent-to-agent chatter; one orchestrator delegating narrow, disposable tasks worked.
Agents misapplied TDD by writing tests layer by layer (horizontal slices); outside-in TDD with vertical slices, bounded execution and fast external feedback worked better.
Rivas cited a study of 660 Claude Code runs: clean code left pass rates unchanged but reduced token use by 7-8% and file revisits by 34%.
The proposed AI harness scorecard checks five pillars: architectural documentation, mechanical constraints, testing and stability, review and risk prevention, and AI-specific safeguards.
takeaways: Turn each recurring agent mistake into a build failure with an actionable message instead of adding another prompt instruction.
Write agent instructions as what to do, not lists of prohibitions.
Have the agent grill you on a story and review the plan before any code is generated.
Wrap flaky environment setup in a script per environment with clear error output so the agent stops burning tokens on it.
Use one orchestrating agent with narrow, disposable sub-agent tasks rather than a team of role-playing agents.

quotes.text: A plausible implementation of the wrong problem is still a wrong solution.
You are anthropomorphizing a human process for a computational system and you will repeat the same pathologies.
We need to let go of the syntax, because now it's the cheapest part of the system that can be built.

watchIf: You need AI-generated code to meet a regulated enterprise's standards and want concrete harness techniques that worked under tight tooling restrictions.
